q: During a real, publicly reported payroll-system outage, a caller says they're from the vendor's incident team, quotes the correct outage ticket number, and asks a clerk to read back the MFA code "to resync the account." What MOST made the caller believable?
w: The credibility came from the made-up but plausible story built on a real event; the phone call is only the channel.
h: Vishing is the phone. Pretexting is the script the actor reads into the phone.

q: An email to accounts payable pretends to be the CEO, references a real acquisition from yesterday's press release, and requests an urgent wire to a "closing escrow account." Which technique is the question really asking about if it says "what made the request seem legitimate"?
w: Phishing is the delivery channel; the believable backstory tied to real news is the pretext.
h: Ask "why did they believe it?" not "how did it arrive?"

q: Users are repeatedly disconnected, then reconnect to a network with the SAME SSID and a stronger signal that shows a login page. The wireless IDS logs a flood of deauthentication frames. What is this?
w: Same SSID plus stronger signal plus forced deauth is the detail that only fits an evil twin.
h: A rogue AP is a stranger in the building. An evil twin is a stranger wearing your coworker's face.

q: Which control BEST stops attackers from forging the deauthentication frames used to push clients onto a look-alike AP?
w: PMF (mandatory in WPA3) authenticates management frames, so deauth frames can't be spoofed.
h: PMF puts a signature on the bouncer's "you're kicked out" notes.

q: A 15-person accounting office with no IT staff wants firewall, gateway antivirus, URL filtering, and site-to-site VPN in one box, managed from one console at a low fixed cost. Which is BEST?
w: Small office + all-in-one + single console + low cost is the UTM tell.
h: UTM is the Swiss Army knife for a small shop. NGFW is the specialist's scalpel.

q: A policy says "data in transit must be protected." A second document says "all external web services must use TLS 1.2 or higher with AES-GCM cipher suites; no exceptions without CISO approval." What is the second document?
w: It names specific protocol versions and ciphers — that makes it a standard.
h: Policy = Purpose. Standard = Specifics. Procedure = Process steps. Guideline = Good idea (optional).

q: A document states "Staff should consider using a password manager for personal accounts." Which document type is it?
w: "Should consider" is a recommendation, not a requirement — guidelines are the only optional type.
h: Guideline = Good idea. Nobody gets written up for ignoring a good idea.

q: User jlee lives in Phoenix. VPN logs show jlee connected from Phoenix 09:00–12:00 and from Tempe 10:30–11:15. Which indicator is this?
w: The cities are next to each other, but the time windows overlap — two people are using one account.
h: Impossible travel is about distance. Concurrent sessions are about overlap. Check the clocks before the map.

q: A logged-in banking customer reads a forum in another tab. A post contains a 1×1 image whose src is https://bank.example.com/transfer?to=88213409&amount=4900, and the money moves. What attack is this?
w: No script runs — the victim's browser is tricked into sending a request and attaches the bank's cookie automatically.
h: CSRF is a forged signature: the attacker writes the check, your browser signs it with your cookie.

q: Which fix BEST prevents the forged transfer request in a CSRF attack like the forum-image one?
o: Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies on the bank's site
A content security policy on the forum
Setting HttpOnly on the bank's session cookie
Input validation on the forum's post field
w: The target site has to protect itself; the attacker controls (or doesn't care about) the forum.
h: You don't fix forged checks by asking the forger's printer shop to behave.

q: Stored XSS on a portal lets a script read the session cookie and send it out. The code fix will take weeks. The cookie is currently: Set-Cookie: SID=7f3c; Secure; SameSite=Lax. Which change BEST reduces impact now?
o: Scope Domain to the portal host only
w: The attack is script reading document.cookie — only HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript.
h: HttpOnly Hides it from script (anti-XSS). SameSite = Stay on this Site (anti-CSRF).

q: A "fetch profile picture from URL" feature receives url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/app-role and returns JSON instead of an image. What attack is this?
w: The server was tricked into fetching an internal-only network address — the cloud metadata service.
h: See 169.254.169.254? Think "SSRF stealing cloud keys" instantly.

q: Which pair of controls BEST mitigates SSRF against the AWS instance metadata service?
o: Require IMDSv2 and allow-list fetch destinations
Add HttpOnly and Secure to session cookies
Enable full-disk encryption on the instance
Deploy anti-CSRF tokens on every form
w: IMDSv2 needs a PUT-issued session token simple SSRF can't get, and an allow-list stops arbitrary internal fetches.
h: Don't let the server accept delivery addresses inside your own building.

q: What happens to traffic from 10.5.5.5 to 172.16.40.20 on TCP 443?
c:
#  Action  Proto  Source  Destination      Port
1  PERMIT  TCP    any     172.16.40.0/24   443
2  DENY    TCP    any     172.16.40.20     443
3  DENY    IP     any     any              any (log)
w: 172.16.40.20 is inside 172.16.40.0/24, so rule 1 matches first and processing stops; rule 2 is shadowed.
h: The bouncer stops reading at the first line that mentions you.

q: Using the same rules, what is the BEST fix so 172.16.40.20 is blocked on 443 while the rest of 172.16.40.0/24 still accepts HTTPS from anywhere?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  any  172.16.40.0/24  443
2  DENY    TCP  any  172.16.40.20    443
3  DENY    IP   any  any             any (log)
o: Change rule 1's source to the internal subnet only
w: Specific before broad; the other options break the "other servers from anywhere" requirement or open everything.
h: A fix that solves one requirement by breaking another is always wrong.

q: An admin deletes the final "DENY IP any any (log)" rule. Traffic matching no other rule arrives. What happens?
o: It's denied by implicit deny, but no log entry is written
It's allowed because nothing denies it
It's denied and logged as before
The firewall fails open until a rule is added
w: Implicit deny still blocks unmatched traffic; the explicit rule existed mainly to log it.
h: Not on the list? You're not getting in — but nobody writes down that you tried.

q: A hospital needs full visibility of core traffic with no added latency and no new point of failure. Which device and placement?
o: IDS on a SPAN port or tap
WAF in front of the core switch
w: A copy of traffic (SPAN/tap) adds no latency and can't take the network down — but it can only alert.
h: IDS = In the Doorway with a Spyglass. It watches a copy and yells.

q: Exploit traffic between the internal firewall and the core must be blocked automatically. Which device and placement?
w: Only a device physically in the traffic path can block it.
h: IPS = In the Path, Stops.

q: Where should a WAF protecting public web servers be placed?
o: In the DMZ right after the perimeter firewall, in front of the web servers
Outside the perimeter firewall, facing the internet
Between the web servers and the database tier only
w: It should inspect web traffic after the firewall drops the junk and before any server sees it.
h: Firewall sweeps the street; WAF checks the guests at the door.

q: Three web servers sit behind a load balancer. Each user's session data lives only in the memory of the server that first handled them, and requests must be spread across all three. Which configuration?
w: Without affinity, users land on a server that doesn't have their session and get logged out.
h: Sticky sessions = you keep the same bank teller, because only that teller has your paperwork.

q: A laptop passes 802.1X authentication but fails NAC posture (missing patches). What should NAC do?
o: Place it in a quarantine/remediation VLAN
Grant full access and alert the SOC
w: Quarantine lets it reach the patch server but not production, so it can fix itself and get in.
h: NAC quarantine is the urgent-care waiting room — not sent home, not let into surgery.

q: A hospital's inline IPS protects clinical systems. Leadership says patient care must never stop if the IPS fails. Which failure mode?
w: Fail-open keeps traffic flowing uninspected — availability wins.
h: Open door = traffic keeps flowing; closed door = everything stops.

q: At 02:31, right after 4.8 GB leaves the network, EDR shows: vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet. What is the attacker MOST likely doing?
c:
02:05  Event ID 4672  svc_backup  special privileges assigned
02:18  rclone.exe  outbound 4.8 GB -> 185.220.101.47
02:31  vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet
w: Deleting shadow copies removes easy restores; privileges were already gained at 4672.
h: Cutting the phone line before kicking in the door — encryption is minutes away.

q: Same incident: the attacker has a foothold on WS-HR-112, the svc_backup credentials, and access to FS-02. What is the BEST containment step?
o: Isolate both hosts with EDR and disable svc_backup
Block 185.220.101.47 at the firewall and keep monitoring
Power off every server in the data center
w: Containment must cover every foothold — hosts and credentials — while keeping RAM evidence intact.
h: Lock every room the burglar is in and take back the key they stole.

q: Which is the BEST hardening for the svc_backup service account after the incident?
o: Restrict logon to the backup server and use a long, auto-rotated password (gMSA)
Lock the account after 5 failed attempts
Require SMS MFA for the account
Rename it to something less obvious
w: Lockout invites a DoS on backups, SMS can't work non-interactively, and renaming is obscurity.
h: A service account should only open one door, with a key that changes itself.

q: Attackers use a reverse-proxy kit (AiTM) that relays logins to the real portal in real time and steals the session cookie. Which MFA BEST stops this even if the admin is fooled?
w: FIDO2 signs a challenge bound to the real domain, so the fake site gets nothing usable.
h: Codes are passwords you say out loud. A FIDO2 key only fits your bank's actual lock.

q: Push notifications with number matching are MOST effective against which attack?
w: Number matching stops blind approval spam, but a user actively logging in to an AiTM site still sees and enters the real number.
h: Number matching stops "approve, approve, approve" — not a user who's being fooled.

q: Clinical Wi-Fi must use device certificates on both sides, no passwords, and allow revoking any single device. Which EAP method?
w: EAP-TLS is mutual certificate auth — the certs are the authentication.
h: EAP-TLS = Two Locks, Server and client.

q: Users join Wi-Fi with their existing AD usernames and passwords, and only the RADIUS server presents a certificate. Which EAP method is MOST likely?
w: PEAP builds a tunnel with a server cert and passes MSCHAPv2 (the password) inside it.
h: PEAP and TTLS build a tunnel, then pass a password through it.

q: A VPN portal certificate is valid, publicly trusted, has a matching wildcard SAN and RSA 3072 — but every client rejects it. What's wrong?
o: It isn't authorized for Server Authentication
The wildcard can't cover a VPN hostname
RSA 3072 is too weak for TLS
It needs the Client Authentication EKU instead
w: A TLS server certificate needs the Server Authentication EKU (…3.1); code signing can't do that job.
h: EKU is the job title on the badge. A valid "Code Signing" badge can't open the server room.

q: A certificate's SAN is *.corp.example.com. Which hostname will FAIL name validation?
w: A wildcard covers exactly one label, so two labels deep doesn't match.
h: The asterisk is one seat at the table, not the whole row.

q: A medication database must be recoverable to any specific minute in the last 24 hours. Last year a bad script's corruption copied to the standby replica instantly. Nightly full backups exist. What should be added?
o: Synchronous replication to a second site
w: Restore the nightly full, then replay the journal to one minute before the bad change; replication copies the damage.
h: Replication is a mirror — it shows the coffee stain too. Journaling is a video you can rewind.

q: The BIA sets an RTO of 4 hours for the core system. Measured MTTR is 12 hours and MTBF is 18 months. What is the conclusion?
o: The RTO can't be met; a standby system or faster SLA is needed
The RTO is met because failures are rare
MTBF offsets the MTTR, so no change is needed
w: Compare the measured average (MTTR) to the target (RTO); how rarely it fails never makes repairs faster.
h: RTO is the deadline. MTTR is how long your homework actually takes.

q: A coding-challenge site runs untrusted submissions. Last month a kernel flaw let processes break out of containers. Modest overhead is acceptable. Which is BEST?
o: Run each submission in its own VM
Containers with a read-only root filesystem
w: Containers share one kernel; VMs each have their own and are isolated by the hypervisor.
h: Containers are apartments on one foundation. VMs are separate houses.

q: A newly provisioned "empty" block storage volume contains another company's database fragments. The provider confirms no hypervisor compromise. What vulnerability is this?
w: Storage was reallocated without being wiped; nothing ran, and the stem ruled out hypervisor compromise.
h: A hotel room that wasn't cleaned — nobody broke in.

q: Forty Kubernetes microservices talk over plain HTTP. Each service must prove its identity to the other, and traffic must be encrypted. Which is BEST?
o: A WAF at the cluster ingress
w: mTLS encrypts east-west traffic and has both sides present certificates; FDE is at rest and a WAF only sees north-south.
h: TLS is the bank showing you its ID. mTLS is both of you showing IDs.

q: EDR shows no files written to disk. What technique does this sequence show?
c:
parent=WINWORD.EXE child=powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
powershell.exe -> OpenProcess(explorer.exe, PROCESS_VM_WRITE|PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD)
powershell.exe -> VirtualAllocEx(explorer.exe, 0x3000, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)
powershell.exe -> CreateRemoteThread(explorer.exe)
w: Code is deliberately written into another process's memory with legitimate APIs and run there — for stealth, not new privileges.
h: A hermit crab moving into a shell everyone already trusts.

q: Each regional office sets its own security policies, chooses its own tools, and controls its own budget; HQ only gets quarterly reports. Auditors find inconsistent controls. Which structure is this?
w: Inconsistent controls across units is the signature weakness of decentralized governance.
h: Every location has its own chef — great local food, but the burgers taste different everywhere.

q: Before awarding a contract, a utility asks bidders where their circuit boards and firmware come from and checks those sub-suppliers against restricted-entity lists. What activity is this?
w: Looking at the vendor's own suppliers and component origins is supply chain analysis; right-to-audit is a post-signing contract term.
h: Ask where the caterer buys their meat before you hire them.

q: Two hospitals form a joint venture and sign a document covering how revenue and costs are split, each partner's responsibilities, and data protection duties. Which agreement?
w: Partners splitting revenue in a joint venture is a business partners agreement; an MSA is a customer buying from a vendor.
h: MSA = landlord and tenant. BPA = co-owners of the building.

q: A company signs a three-year umbrella contract with a consultancy setting payment terms and liability, then signs a separate document for each project with deliverables and timelines. What is the per-project document?
w: The umbrella is the MSA; each project's deliverables live in a statement of work.
h: MSA is the umbrella; SOWs are the people standing under it.

q: Customer personal data is spread across a CRM, a marketing platform, ticket attachments, and analysts' spreadsheets, and no one can confirm everywhere it's stored. What should be built FIRST?
w: "Where is it stored?" is answered by the inventory; everything else builds on it.
h: You can't clean the house if you don't know which rooms you own.

q: An EU customer submits a valid erasure request. You hold their marketing preferences, support chat transcripts, and invoices that tax law requires keeping for seven years. What is the BEST response?
o: Delete preferences and transcripts; retain invoices with use restricted to the tax obligation
Deny the request because some data must be kept
Anonymize the invoices and delete everything else
Delete all of it, including the invoices
w: The legal-obligation exception covers only the data the law requires; anonymizing breaks the requirement for original invoices.
h: Clean out the closet, except what the IRS says to keep — and lock that box.

q: A small windowless server room has constant cooling airflow and a thin wall next to a busy hallway. Which motion sensor BEST detects a person after hours with few false alarms?
w: Airflow rules out ultrasonic, the thin wall rules out microwave, and a pressure mat covers one spot.
h: Read the environment clues as eliminators — what's left is the answer.

q: The exam opens with five long PBQs. With 90 minutes for 90 questions, what is the BEST approach?
o: Flag the PBQs, do all multiple choice first, return with ~25 minutes left
Finish each PBQ fully before moving on
Skip PBQs entirely since they're worth the same as MCQs
Spend 2–3 minutes per MCQ to avoid careless errors
w: Points lost to the clock need no new knowledge; PBQs give partial credit when rushed, blank MCQs give zero.
h: Bank the quick points first, then go back for the heavy lifting.
